papers_read.title_as_printed: Combined mind-body physical exercise, cognitive training, and nurse-led risk factor modification to enhance cognition among older adults with mild cognitive impairment in primary care: a three-arm randomised controlled trial (Xu et al., Lancet Healthy Longev 2025; 6: 100706)
Non-pharmacological interventions for mild cognitive impairment: a review of social, cognitive, and physical stimulation strategies (Berardi and Sale, Brain and Environment 4 (2025) 100010)

what_each_reports.P-895: 456 randomised (423 analysed) Hong Kong primary-care adults aged 60-80 with HK-MoCA 19-25. Arms: CPR (Tai Chi 30 min and group cognitive leisure activities 1 h, each 3x/week for 12 weeks, plus quarterly nurse-led risk-factor modification), RFM alone, health-advice pamphlets. Primary ADAS-Cog Z at 15 months: CPR vs health advice beta -0.04 (95% CI -0.34 to 0.26), RFM vs health advice -0.14 (-0.44 to 0.15), CPR vs RFM 0.10 (-0.19 to 0.40), Bonferroni-corrected; also null at 6 and 12 months and on all secondary outcomes. Attendance 59%/58% of Tai Chi/cognitive sessions. All three groups improved within-group. Per-protocol and subgroup signals (hypertension, GDS >= 5) favoured CPR at 6 months.
what_each_reports.P-914: Narrative review (PubMed/Scopus, 2013-2024; no pooled estimate, no systematic selection) of social, cognitive and physical stimulation in MCI. States that combining modalities 'may yield additive or synergistic benefits', citing Gates et al. (2019), FINGER (at-risk adults with normal-range cognition) and Train the Brain (MCI). Also states: 'Notably, not all interventions have yielded positive outcomes. Several randomized controlled trials have reported modest or non-significant cognitive improvements, especially in short-duration or low-intensity programs.'

quantity_a: Between-group difference in ADAS-Cog Z score at 15 months for a specific 3-month cognitive-leisure plus Tai Chi programme with quarterly nurse-led risk-factor modification, versus nurse-led risk-factor modification alone and versus health-advice pamphlets, in Hong Kong primary-care MCI (modified ITT, Bonferroni).
quantity_b: No estimand: a qualitative, hedged judgement that multimodal (social, cognitive, physical) programmes may yield additive or synergistic benefits over single-domain approaches, drawn from heterogeneous trials of mostly longer or more intensive programmes, including FINGER in non-MCI at-risk adults.
incompatible_if_same: No. P-914 reports no effect size, so no estimate exists whose uncertainty could exclude P-895's; and at the level of claims P-914 itself says short-duration or low-intensity trials have produced non-significant results, which is what P-895's authors report for their 3-month active phase with about 58% attendance.

gates.dataset_family: mismatch: P-914's source literature (2013-2024) does not include P-895 (published April 2025) and rests largely on FINGER and Train the Brain; no shared trial.
gates.validation_tier: match as coded (V2 both); neither validates a predictive model.
gates.modality_family: partial: both concern multimodal non-pharmacological programmes in MCI, but P-914 covers social, cognitive and physical stimulation in general while P-895's 'cognitive training' is group leisure activities (mahjong, reading, calligraphy) plus Tai Chi for 12 weeks. Study-design gate (RCT vs narrative review) fails with no waiver on record.

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: P-895 reports a single pre-specified ADAS-Cog Z-score contrast against an active health-advice control; P-914 reports no metric and compares multimodal programmes with single-domain or usual-care conditions across heterogeneous outcomes.
independence: Independent: distinct authors; P-895 postdates P-914's search window and is not cited by it.
grounds: P-914 is a narrative review that reports no pooled or trial-level estimate, so there is no quantity on its side that P-895's confidence intervals could contradict.

The comparison differs: P-914's claim concerns multimodal versus single-domain programmes, mostly longer ones and anchored on FINGER in non-MCI at-risk adults, whereas P-895 tests a 3-month leisure-cognitive plus Tai Chi package with quarterly nurse visits against a health-advice pamphlet control.

P-914 itself notes that short-duration or low-intensity trials have produced non-significant results, which is the category P-895's authors place their own trial in (3-month active phase, about 58% attendance), so even at claim level the two statements can both be true.
The study-design gate (RCT vs narrative review) fails and no waiver is on record; the C-227 waiver concerned a network meta-analysis with estimates, which P-914 does not have.

evidence_quotes.quote: No significant difference between the three groups in ADAS-Cog was found at the primary endpoint at 15 months (CPR vs health advice, β= –0⋅04 [95% CI –0⋅34 to 0⋅26]; RFM vs health advice, β= –0⋅14 [–0⋅44 to 0⋅15]; CPR vs RFM, β=0⋅10 [–0⋅19 to 0⋅40]) nor at the 6-month and 12-month follow-ups.
In the CPR group, participants attended a mean of 59% (36) of the 36 Tai Chi sessions and 58% (37) of the 36 cognitive sessions.
the relatively short intervention period of 3 months and low compliance with the intervention might have affected the study results.

These were leisure activities that required higher cognitive efforts, including reading newspapers, books, or magazines; using computers and browsing the internet; playing mahjong, board games, or card games

emerging evidence suggests that combining social, cognitive, and physical stimulation into integrated multimodal interventions may yield additive or synergistic benefits for cognitive health in older adults with MCI.

Notably, not all interventions have yielded positive outcomes. Several randomized controlled trials have reported modest or non-significant cognitive improvements, especially in short-duration or low-intensity programs
can significantly improve or maintain cognitive functions in at-risk elderly populations with cognition within the normal range for age.
We acknowledge that narrative synthesis may introduce selection bias

record_defects: The record quotes P-914 as saying multimodal combinations 'produce additive/synergistic benefits'; the PDF says they 'may yield additive or synergistic benefits', a hedged claim.
The record omits that P-914 explicitly concedes non-significant results in short-duration or low-intensity trials, which removes the claim-level contradiction for a 3-month programme.

The record describes P-895's CPR as 'cognitive training'; the PDF specifies group leisure activities (reading, mahjong, calligraphy, crafts), not structured cognitive training of the kind cited by P-914 (Gates et al., Train the Brain).

The record says P-895 tests 'exactly that intervention shape'; the control arm also received baseline nurse health advice and blood-test feedback, and the active phase was 12 weeks, which differs from the programmes P-914 cites (FINGER 2 years; FINGER population was not MCI).

The record does not mention P-895's per-protocol (CDR-SOB at 6 months) and subgroup (hypertension, GDS >= 5) findings favouring CPR, which the authors present as exploratory and which bear on how 'flatly null' the trial is.
what_would_change_the_verdict: A meta-analysis in the corpus reporting a pooled estimate for comparable multimodal programmes (similar dose and comparator) in MCI on a global cognition endpoint whose interval excludes P-895's estimate; P-914 provides no estimate.
